processing: Not a leaf style but a way of cooking tea: leaves are boiled in a small pot with water, and in the best-known version a flour batter, oil, spices and salt are stirred in.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest; it is cooked all year, and is especially welcome in winter.
appearance_dry: Plain local tea leaf, with the seasonings and additions kept separately until cooking.
appearance_liquor: A thick, opaque, savoury brown broth when made with batter.
appearance_wet: The leaves stay in the pot among the batter and toppings and are not the point of the dish.
taste_profile: Savoury and warming, with tea, fennel, Korean mint and ginger in a thick soup, plus crunchy toppings.

brewing.notes: Amounts are a rough guide, since home cooks work by eye. Half fill a small pot, boil the leaves, stir in flour batter and oil, then season with fennel, Korean mint, ginger and salt. Add walnuts, diced meat or egg as you like.

vintage_note: It is not sold by season or year. It is a dish made at home and at food stalls from ordinary local tea, so any fresh-enough leaf will do and no vintage applies.
description:
Guanguan tea is a tea snack from Lüeyang county in southern Shaanxi, closer to a savoury porridge than a cup of tea. A small pot goes on the fire and everything happens inside it. It is listed as provincial intangible cultural heritage.

There are several forms: plain water-boiled tea, oil-fried tea and batter tea. The batter version is the famous one, with flour batter and oil added as the leaves boil, then fennel, Korean mint, ginger and salt, and often walnuts, diced meat or egg.

It is thick, salty and warming, with crunchy bits on top and toasted bread on the side. Locals drink it first thing in the morning or when guests arrive, and it is especially good in cold weather.

You will not find a tea to buy under this name. To try it, go to Lüeyang's food stalls or make it at home with any plain green tea.
history:
Little reliable history is recorded. The custom is usually traced to the eating habits of the Di and Qiang peoples, a tradition passed on by word of mouth rather than a dated record.

It survives as everyday food in Lüeyang's towns and villages, and local rhymes still describe the method step by step.
